nameStory: The Korean Euodia gets its name from its native homeland of Korea, though it's also found in southwestern China. It's sometimes called the 'bee-bee tree' because of the incredible buzz that fills the air when its flowers are in bloom - thousands of bees and other pollinators create such a loud hum that you can hear the tree from quite a distance!
description: Korean Euodia is a medium-sized deciduous tree that can grow 30-50 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. It belongs to the citrus family, which might surprise you since it's not producing oranges or lemons! The tree has compound leaves that give off a subtle citrusy scent when crushed, and it produces clusters of small, creamy white flowers in late summer that are absolutely beloved by bees and butterflies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 5-11 leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, opposite each other on the branch. Crush a leaf and smell - you'll detect a faint citrusy, almost lemony scent that hints at its citrus family heritage.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny creamy white flowers appear in late summer (July-August), each flower only about 1/4 inch across but packed together in showy 4-6 inch wide displays that buzz loudly with pollinator activity.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small reddish-brown to black capsules split open to reveal shiny black seeds, clustered together where the flowers were. The seed clusters persist into fall and can help with winter identification.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray bark when young that develops shallow furrows and a slightly corky texture as the tree matures, somewhat similar to ash tree bark but typically smoother overall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a broad, rounded canopy with sturdy branches that spread wide. Young trees may be more upright, but mature specimens develop an attractive vase-like or umbrella-shaped silhouette.

habitat: In New England, Korean Euodia is found primarily in cultivated settings like parks, arboretums, and residential landscapes where it's been planted as an ornamental tree. It adapts well to various soil types and urban conditions, though it prefers well-drained soils and full to partial sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, showing fresh bright green compound foliage. The citrusy scent becomes noticeable when leaves are crushed.
seasonality.summer: The tree's glory season - dense clusters of creamy white flowers appear in late summer, creating an impressive pollinator magnet that fills the air with buzzing sounds.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and the reddish-brown seed clusters become prominent, often persisting after leaf fall for easy identification.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the smooth gray bark and persistent seed clusters. The opposite branching pattern and distinctive bark help with identification.

funFact: A single Korean Euodia tree in full bloom can sound like it's housing an entire bee colony - the flowers are so irresistible to pollinators that the collective buzzing can be heard from over 100 feet away, making it one of the loudest trees in the forest during late summer!
confusionNotes: Korean Euodia's compound leaves might be confused with ash trees, but ash trees have 7-9 leaflets that are more lance-shaped, and ash trees definitely don't smell citrusy when you crush the leaves. Remember: if it smells lemony and blooms in late summer with bee-magnet flowers, you've found a Korean Euodia!
contextualKnowledge: You might see this tree listed under different names in older gardening books - it was formerly called Euodia hupehensis or classified in the genus Evodia. The name changes reflect ongoing botanical research, but the tree remains the same wonderful pollinator magnet regardless of what scientists decide to call it!
compareHints: Korean Euodia is the only Tetradium species commonly found in New England landscapes. Within the citrus family, it's most likely to be confused with other compound-leaved trees, but most citrus family members in our region are shrubs or small trees, and none have the same late-summer flowering spectacle that makes Korean Euodia such a standout pollinator tree.
